p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the difference between a warehouse and a distribution center?
t: A warehouse mainly stores goods; a distribution center moves them quickly. Distribution centers typically have more dock doors, deeper truck courts, trailer parking, employees, and conveyors because inventory turns over in days rather than months. Many buildings serve either use; dock count, court depth, and parking help determine fit.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is flex space?
t: Flex space combines substantial finished office or showroom area (often a quarter or more) with warehouse, lab, or light assembly space. It usually has lower clear heights and more grade-level doors than a warehouse, suiting companies that need offices and goods under one roof. See flex space in the glossary .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is small-bay industrial?
t: Small-bay (or shallow-bay) industrial divides a building into suites, often a few thousand to roughly 25,000 square feet, for contractors, service businesses, distributors, and light manufacturers. Suites typically have an office, drive-in or dock door, and separate utilities. Few new small-bay buildings are built, supporting a deep local market for 10,000 to 100,000 SF properties.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a last-mile industrial facility?
t: A last-mile (or last-touch) facility is a warehouse or service building near dense population for final delivery to homes and businesses. Proximity to customers, labor, and arterial roads, plus van and fleet parking, matters more than size or height. Infill sites near Chicago and inner-ring suburbs are typical locations.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is industrial outdoor storage (IOS)?
t: Industrial outdoor storage is land for parking trucks and trailers, staging equipment, or storing materials, usually on a fenced, lit paved or gravel surface with little or no building. Value depends on zoning, access, surfacing, stormwater compliance, and scarcity; many municipalities restrict it. See IOS in the glossary .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is cold storage, and why is it different?
t: Cold storage is a temperature-controlled warehouse for refrigerated or frozen goods. Insulated panels, refrigeration systems, freezer-grade floors with under-slab heating, heavy power, and specialized docks make it far more expensive to build and convert than a dry warehouse. That cost, plus food-safety requirements, keeps supply limited and tenants sticky.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What do Class A, B, and C mean for industrial buildings?
t: Building class broadly describes age and functionality. Class A buildings are newer, with modern clear heights, ESFR sprinklers, deep truck courts, and wide columns; Class B buildings are older but functional; Class C buildings have limits such as low clear height, tight columns, or poor access. Class is not standardized, so compare specifications. See industrial building classes .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who leases and owns industrial buildings?
t: Tenants include manufacturers, distributors, third-party logistics (3PL) providers, e-commerce and retail companies, contractors, food and beverage firms, and service businesses. Owners range from owner-users who occupy their buildings to private investors, family offices, syndicators, private equity funds, institutional investors, and publicly traded REITs. In the 10,000 to 100,000 SF range, owner-users and private investors are the most common buyers.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a truck court, and how deep should it be?
t: The truck court is the paved maneuvering and parking area before dock doors. Modern single-sided courts commonly measure 120 to 135 feet, with more depth needed when trucks use both sides. Shallow courts limit truck access and are hard to fix. See truck court . These are screening examples, not safe-clearance guarantees. Review the sourced vehicle dimensions and turning-path reference and have a qualified engineer check the fleet's entry, backing, and exit paths.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Why does column spacing matter in an industrial building?
t: Column spacing affects how efficiently racking, aisles, and equipment fit. Wider spacing adds flexibility; tight spacing wastes floor area and may rule out users. Modern buildings commonly use 50-foot bays with deeper speed bays at docks. See column spacing .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an ESFR sprinkler system?
t: ESFR (early suppression, fast response) is a ceiling sprinkler system designed to suppress high-piled storage fires without in-rack sprinklers in many configurations. Adequacy depends on commodity, storage and building height, and water supply; a fire-protection engineer should confirm fit for each tenant. See ESFR sprinklers .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How much electrical power does an industrial building need?
t: Lighting and battery charging may need modest service; manufacturing, cold storage, and EV fleets may need much more. Service is described by amperage, voltage, and phase; three-phase is standard for motors and machinery. Confirm capacity with an electrician and utility, as upgrades can take months. See three-phase power .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What should I know about the floor slab?
t: Slab thickness, reinforcement, load capacity, and flatness matter for racking, forklifts, and machinery. Tall racks and narrow-aisle equipment need level floors; heavy manufacturing needs high load capacity. Review drawings and visible cracking or joint failure, and have an engineer assess demanding uses. See slab load and flatness .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How much office space is typical in an industrial building?
t: Warehouse and distribution buildings often have under 10 to 15 percent office; flex buildings may have more. Excess office raises costs, may sit empty, and narrows the tenant pool. Match office area to local users. See office finish percentage .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How long are industrial leases?
t: Industrial leases are commonly three to ten years. Small-bay and small-business tenants often sign three- to five-year terms, while large distribution and build-to-suit leases can run ten years or longer. Longer terms usually come with more landlord-funded improvements and free rent; shorter terms keep the tenant flexible. Renewal options extend the term at the tenant’s choice.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do rent escalations work in industrial leases?
t: Base rent usually rises by a fixed percentage or amount per square foot; some leases use CPI or stepped increases. Escalations compound, so model total rent over the term. See escalations .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a tenant improvement (TI) allowance?
t: A TI allowance funds tenant build-out or modifications such as offices, electrical, lighting, restrooms, or dock work. Usually quoted per square foot, it reflects lease term and credit and is recovered through rent. Clarify construction management and treatment of unused funds. See TI allowance .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How is industrial rent quoted?
t: Industrial rent is usually quoted in dollars per square foot per year on a net basis, with taxes, insurance, and CAM separate. Smaller suites may be quoted as monthly gross rent. Confirm whether a quote is net or gross, annual or monthly, and ask for current expense estimates.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays for the roof, HVAC, and structural repairs in an industrial lease?
t: It depends on the lease. Commonly, tenants handle routine repairs and maintenance of their space and HVAC, while landlords keep responsibility for roof replacement and structure. However, some “absolute NNN” leases shift everything to the tenant. Read who repairs and who replaces, and whether replacement costs can be amortized into CAM.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What should I ask before leasing a warehouse?
t: Confirm zoning allows your use; clear height, door types and count, truck-court depth, and trailer parking; electrical service; sprinkler adequacy for your storage; office and restroom count; current taxes, insurance, and CAM; repair and replacement responsibilities; renewal and expansion rights; restoration obligations at move-out; and access hours, security, and outdoor storage rights. The tour checklist covers what to measure.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Should a business lease or buy its industrial building?
t: Buying offers control, equity, rent-increase protection, and a long-term asset, but ties up capital and adds concentration and repair risk. Leasing preserves cash and flexibility. Stable businesses with specialized improvements may buy, sometimes using SBA 504 financing; fast-growing firms often lease. Compare both over the same horizon with your accountant.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a build-to-suit?
t: A build-to-suit is designed for a specific tenant or buyer, usually committed before construction. The user gets needed specifications in exchange for a long lease or purchase commitment; the developer reduces leasing risk. Site selection, entitlements, design, and construction often take a year or more.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a speculative (spec) industrial building?
t: A speculative (spec) building is built without a signed tenant, in anticipation of demand. Generic modern standards suit many users and allow faster occupancy than a build-to-suit, while adding supply that can affect submarket rents.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an industrial sublease, and is it a good option?
t: A sublease lets a new occupant use some or all of a tenant’s space, usually with landlord consent. It may cost less and include furniture or racking, but is limited to the original lease term and depends on the tenant remaining in good standing. Read the master lease.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What security deposit or guaranty will an industrial landlord ask for?
t: Security reflects tenant finances, time in business, lease term, and landlord costs for improvements and commissions. Expect a cash deposit or letter of credit; newer or smaller tenants may also need a personal or corporate guaranty. Negotiate a burn-down after on-time payments.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays the broker on an industrial lease?
t: In most commercial leases the landlord pays leasing commissions under its listing agreement, and a tenant’s broker is typically paid from that commission. Arrangements vary, so ask how each broker is compensated and confirm any agency disclosures Illinois requires. See leasing commission .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a letter of intent (LOI) in commercial real estate?
t: A letter of intent summarizes price or rent, term, contingencies, timing, and key conditions before drafting the purchase agreement or lease. Business terms are usually non-binding, though confidentiality or exclusivity may bind. Clear terms reduce surprises. See LOI .

h: How do I start investing in industrial real estate?
t: Options range from public industrial REITs and passive syndications or funds to direct ownership. Direct buyers often start with a small single-tenant or small-bay building in a familiar market, build a team (broker, attorney, lender, inspectors, accountant), and learn to analyze leases and operating statements before making offers.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an industrial REIT?
t: An industrial REIT owns and usually operates industrial properties, distributing most taxable income to shareholders. Public REITs offer liquidity and diversification but no control over individual buildings, and share prices move with the market. Direct ownership offers control and tax-planning options but less liquidity.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What do core, value-add, and opportunistic mean?
t: They describe risk strategies. Core is stabilized, well-located property with long leases and low leverage. Core-plus adds modest upside. Value-add involves leasing up vacancy, renovating, or re-tenanting to raise income. Opportunistic includes development, heavy repositioning, or distressed situations with the highest risk and expected return. See value-add vs. core .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the difference between an owner-user and an investor buyer?
t: An owner-user buys a building to occupy it, valuing location, layout, and control; an investor buys for the income from tenants. Owner-users can sometimes pay more for a vacant or soon-to-be-vacant building, especially with SBA 504 financing, while investors pay for leases in place. Which buyer pool fits a building affects pricing and marketing strategy. See owner-user vs. investor .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a 1031 exchange, and how does it work for industrial property?
t: A Section 1031 exchange can defer federal capital gains tax when proceeds from an investment property sale are reinvested in another qualifying property. IRS rules generally require identification within 45 days and acquisition within 180 days, with proceeds held by a qualified intermediary. Industrial property may be exchanged for other real property held for investment or business use. Consult a tax advisor. See 1031 exchange .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a sale-leaseback?
t: In a sale-leaseback, a business sells the building it occupies to an investor and simultaneously signs a long-term lease to stay. The seller converts real estate equity into working capital while keeping operations in place; the buyer gets a leased property with a known tenant. The rent and lease terms drive the price. See the selling guide’s sale-leaseback section .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do you finance an industrial property purchase?
t: Sources include banks, credit unions, life companies, CMBS lenders, debt funds, and SBA 504 or 7(a) loans for owner-users. Lenders test LTV, debt-service coverage, and sometimes debt yield, as well as lease term, tenant credit, and environmental reports. Compare rate, term, amortization, recourse, reserves, and prepayment terms. See financing in the investment guide .

h: What are DSCR and LTV?
t: DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) is NOI divided by annual loan payments; lenders commonly want a cushion above 1.0, often around 1.25 or higher. LTV (loan-to-value) is the loan amount divided by the property’s value. The lower of the two tests usually sets the maximum loan. See DSCR and LTV .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What are IRR, equity multiple, and cash-on-cash return?
t: Cash-on-cash is annual pre-tax cash flow divided by equity invested. Equity multiple is total cash returned divided by equity over the hold. IRR annualizes returns based on the timing of all cash flows, including sale proceeds. Each measures something different. See IRR .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do you determine market rent for an industrial building?
t: Market rent comes from signed leases for comparable space (size, location, clear height, doors, office, and condition), adjusted for free rent and improvement allowances. Asking rents show expectations, not deals. Ask brokers or appraisers for lease comparables.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do interest rates affect industrial property values?
t: Higher interest rates raise borrowing costs and investors’ required returns, which tends to push cap rates up and prices down unless rents grow enough to offset it. Lower rates generally do the opposite. The effect is not one-for-one: rent growth, supply, and investor demand also matter. Model financing at realistic rates, not the lowest available.

h: Is it better to sell an industrial building vacant or leased?
t: Vacant buildings may attract owner-users willing to pay a premium for the right location and function; leased buildings attract income buyers. Long, market-rate leases often command stronger investor pricing. Short or below-market leases can hurt both buyer pools.

h: What does an industrial investment sales broker do?

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Should I sell off-market or with a full marketing process?
t: Broad marketing reaches more buyers and may produce a stronger price. Off-market offers privacy, less tenant disruption, and speed, but can leave money on the table. A short list of qualified buyers is a middle path. See confidentiality and marketing .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What taxes apply when I sell an industrial building?
t: Federal capital gains tax generally applies to the gain, and depreciation taken is recaptured. For real property, unrecaptured Section 1250 gain is taxed at a federal rate of up to 25 percent. Illinois income tax and, in some cases, the net investment income tax may also apply, and state, county, and local transfer taxes are due at closing. A 1031 exchange can defer gain. Plan with a tax advisor before you list.

h: What happens after I accept an offer on my industrial property?

After diligence, the deposit is typically non-refundable except under specified conditions; the buyer finalizes financing and closes. See PSA and earnest money .

t: A Phase II samples soil, groundwater, vapor, or building materials to test suspected contamination flagged in a Phase I. It is common at sites with historic manufacturing, tanks, dry cleaning, or chemical use. Results may lead to remediation, price changes, insurance, or withdrawal.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What are common environmental issues at industrial sites?
t: Frequent issues include leaking underground or aboveground storage tanks, chlorinated solvents from degreasing, petroleum, metals, PCBs in older equipment, asbestos and lead in building materials, vapor intrusion, fill material of unknown origin, and emerging contaminants such as PFAS. Adjacent properties can also contaminate a site through groundwater.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a property condition assessment?
t: A property condition assessment is an engineer’s review of a building’s roof, structure, paving, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, fire protection, and accessibility, with estimated repair costs and a replacement schedule. For industrial buildings, pay special attention to roof age, dock equipment, slab, sprinklers, and truck-court pavement. See physical diligence .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an ALTA survey, and why do lenders want one?
t: An ALTA/NSPS survey maps boundaries, easements, encroachments, improvements, access, and flood zone to national standards, helping a title insurer remove the standard survey exception. Lenders typically require one. It can confirm truck access, parking, rail spurs, and property-line conflicts. See ALTA survey .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What does a title commitment show, and what does title insurance cover?
t: A title commitment lists the owner, legal description, liens, easements, restrictions, and closing requirements. Title insurance covers certain non-excluded defects, such as forged documents or undisclosed liens. Review each exception; easements and restrictions can limit site use. See title commitment .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a tenant estoppel certificate?
t: An estoppel certificate is a signed statement from a tenant confirming key lease facts: rent, term, deposits, options, amendments, and whether either party is in default. Buyers and lenders rely on estoppels to confirm that the leases match what the seller represented. See estoppel certificate .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an Illinois No Further Remediation (NFR) letter?
t: An NFR letter is issued by the Illinois EPA, typically through its Site Remediation Program or leaking UST program, after a site meets cleanup objectives for a defined use. It often includes land-use restrictions or engineered barriers that must be maintained and recorded. Read the conditions before assuming a site is “clean” for every use.

h: What is the difference between a special use and a variance?
t: A special or conditional use is allowed after public review, often with conditions. A variance grants relief from a standard such as setback, parking, or height when strict application creates hardship. Both require applications and hearings, so allow time. See special use and variance .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is different about industrial property in unincorporated areas?
t: County rules govern zoning, permits, and often utilities and police outside municipal boundaries. Rules and costs may differ from a neighboring village, and annexation can change them. Confirm jurisdiction and utilities. See unincorporated vs. incorporated .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How are industrial property taxes calculated in Illinois?
t: The assessor estimates market value and applies an assessment level; a state or county equalization factor may follow. After exemptions, multiply assessed value by the combined rates of local taxing districts, whose levies set the rates. See the property tax guide .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Why are Cook County industrial property taxes different from the collar counties?
t: Cook County assesses industrial property at 25 percent of market value, reassesses by region every three years, and applies a state equalizer. Other counties generally use one-third of market value, township assessors, and annual equalization. District tax rates also differ. See Cook vs. collar counties .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the Cook County Class 6b incentive?
t: Class 6b lowers assessments for qualifying new, substantially rehabilitated, or reoccupied industrial property. The level is commonly 10 percent of market value for ten years, then 15 and 20 percent in the final two years, versus 25 percent standard. Municipal support and timely application are required. Confirm current rules with the Cook County Assessor. See Cook County incentives .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do I appeal industrial property taxes in Illinois?
t: In Cook County, appeal to the Assessor during the township window, then the Board of Review; elsewhere, appeal to the county Board of Review. Further appeals may go to the state Property Tax Appeal Board or circuit court. Deadlines are short; income, comparable sales, vacancy, or appraisal evidence matters. See appeals and deadlines .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays real estate transfer tax in Illinois?
t: Illinois and counties impose transfer taxes; some municipalities, including Chicago, add one. Sellers usually pay state and county taxes by custom, but local ordinances determine municipal tax responsibility; Chicago’s falls largely on buyers. Confirm current rates and exemptions with your attorney and municipality. See transfer tax .

A functional suite in a liquid submarket is its own credit support.

h: How do I underwrite rollover and downtime realistically?
t: Model each lease expiration instead of using a blended vacancy factor. p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
h: What should I know about flood and stormwater for Chicago-area industrial sites?
t: Check the FEMA flood map first, then the local stormwater rules: in Cook County the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District administers a watershed management ordinance, and the collar counties and municipalities have their own requirements. Detention obligations can affect expansion plans and yard surfacing, and a flat, paved industrial site is not immune to drainage problems.

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
h: Illinois taxes and incentives
t: Will my purchase trigger a reassessment, and how do I underwrite it? A recorded Illinois sale can inform assessed value. Cook County reassesses by region every three years; collar counties use their own cycles with annual equalization. Underwrite your likely post-sale tax bill, not the seller’s, and confirm leases allow recovery of increases. Build an appeal calendar during diligence. The property tax guide links all nine county assessment offices. Does a Cook County Class 6b incentive stay with the property when it sells? Do not assume it. Confirm with the Cook County Assessor’s current incentive bulletins how much of the reduced-assessment schedule remains, what a change in ownership or occupancy requires, whether renewal needs a new municipal resolution, and what conditions could end it. Underwrite the deal with and without the incentive, and treat the difference as negotiable risk. How does a TIF district affect an industrial owner? You pay taxes normally; the district redirects the increment above a base to fund public purposes, often under redevelopment agreements. The practical questions are whether any agreement binds the property, when the district expires, and whether incentives you are counting on depend on it. Read the governing documents rather than the map legend.

p: What experienced industrial investors ask, and how to think about the answers
h: Debt and capital
t: How do lenders size loans on small industrial buildings, and what trips borrowers up? Lenders test loan-to-value, debt service coverage, and often debt yield using their own income and expense definitions. Common hurdles include leases shorter than the loan (requiring rollover reserves or structure), environmental findings, appraisal gaps, recourse, and prepayment limits. Confirm definitions early and model the lender’s case. The debt-service calculator shows the arithmetic. How should I think about refinancing risk at loan maturity? Test whether the property still carries itself with a higher rate, lower loan amount, and tougher appraisal. Usual defenses include moderate leverage, staggered maturities, extension options, and a capital plan independent of cash-out proceeds. When does SBA 504 financing matter to an investor? It matters because owner-users compete for the same buildings. A company planning to occupy most of a building can often finance it through the SBA 504 program with a long-term fixed-rate component, which lets it pay a price an investor cannot justify on rent alone. Expect that competition on vacant or soon-to-be-vacant buildings, and expect it to disappear on buildings with long leases in place.

h: Timing, exit, and sourcing
t: How do I decide between selling, refinancing, and holding? Start with upcoming rollover, roof or pavement costs, loan maturity, tax basis, an exchange plan, and liquidity. Who is the likely buyer of my building at exit? For 10,000 to 100,000 SF buildings, likely buyers include owner-users, private investors, exchange buyers, and smaller funds. p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: Why type and spec matter for 10,000 to 100,000 SF buildings
t: Buyers in the 10,000 to 100,000 square foot range include owner-users and private investors; tenants are often local or regional. The same building may be an operating facility, income investment, or re-tenanting opportunity. Owner-users assess doors, power, production flow, office area, parking, and expansion room. Tenants compare occupancy cost, timing, lease obligations, and operational disruption. Investors review the lease and potential replacement users. The industrial building evaluation checklist and seller guide focus on function, records, and verifiable facts. Function: Does the building support the use without unusual workarounds? Flexibility: Could another user occupy it if the first plan changes? Risk: Are there physical, zoning, environmental, or utility constraints that affect timing or cost?

h: Specifications explained and why each matters
t: Explain each specification's practical effect and separate measured facts from assumptions or broker shorthand. Clear height Clear height is usually measured from the finished floor to the lowest obstruction, not the roof deck. It affects racking, equipment, lighting, and sprinklers; check beams, joists, ducts, heaters, fans, and piping. Column spacing and speed bays Spacing affects storage, forklift movement, production cells, and demising. Speed bays can add dock staging depth; verify dimensions and obstructions. Dock-high doors and door ratio Dock-high loading supports trailer-height movement, often critical for distribution. Door-to-area ratios compare loading intensity, but the right ratio depends on operations, trailer dwell, staffing, and scheduling. Drive-in doors These admit vehicles, equipment, or vans at grade. Verify clear opening, apron slope, condition, security, and safe use across grade changes. Dock levelers, seals, shelters, and bumpers These affect safety, weather protection, handling, and efficiency. Review condition, capacity, controls, and maintenance records. p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: Class A, B, and C as informal labels
t: Industrial class labels are market shorthand, not a single official standard. They can be useful only when tied to facts that can be inspected and documented. Informal ways people describe industrial building class Label Common description Caution Class A Newer or recently modernized building with stronger loading, height, systems, truck circulation, life-safety features, and institutional-quality records. A small Class A building may still be wrong for a user if doors, power, or zoning do not fit. Class B Functional building with some older features, moderate office finish, usable loading, and a condition profile that may require selective capital work. Class B can be a broad category, so list the actual strengths and weaknesses. Class C Older or more specialized building with lower clear height, limited loading, heavier deferred maintenance, or narrower reuse. Class C does not mean unusable; it means the buyer pool may be more specific and diligence may be more important.

p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: How specs translate to buyer and tenant pools
t: Specifications determine who can operate efficiently. Strong doors, turning, power, and fire protection may broaden distribution or manufacturing demand compared with a similarly sized building with limited utility. Functional obsolescence is a mismatch with current operating needs, such as low clear height, shallow truck courts, insufficient power, limited parking, excess office finish, difficult column spacing, or loading unsuited to building size. Investors assess re-tenanting risk by estimating the potential user pool, improvement timing, and required capital. See the investment diligence guide and commercial leasing guide . Broader pool: flexible layout, adequate power, code-compliant improvements, documented systems, and common loading patterns. Narrower pool: very specialized equipment, unusual floor plan, unresolved environmental history, nonconforming yard, or limited truck access. Seller takeaway: disclose constraints clearly and support strengths with records rather than adjectives.

t: A tractor alone includes the cab and power unit; wheelbase, axle layout, sleeper, and fifth-wheel position vary. A tractor plus semitrailer is an articulated combination whose overall length depends on both vehicles and their connection. Do not add a guessed tractor length to a trailer label or treat it as overall rig length. p: Truck dimensions and turning paths
h: Turning circle, swept path, and offtracking
t: Turning circle diameter vs. radius Diameter spans a circle; radius is half only when both use the same circle and measurement convention. A curb-to-curb wheel path is not a wall-to-wall body envelope. Ask which reference point, steering lock, speed, and maneuver were measured. Swept path and outer sweep A swept path is the area a vehicle occupies during a maneuver. Its outer boundary includes front corners, mirrors, body overhang, and trailer swing, not just tire tracks. Offtracking Rear wheels and a trailer do not follow the tractor's front-wheel path in a low-speed turn; they commonly track inward. Trailer length, wheelbase, axle locations, articulation, steering, and approach angle change the path. Design vehicle AASHTO labels such as WB-62 and WB-67 describe specific geometric templates, not interchangeable fleet measurements or a universal radius. A qualified engineer must select a current design vehicle and compare it with the site's fleet and maneuvers. No turning radius is given because the cited fleet specifications do not establish one for a complete configuration. Forward circulation, backing into a dock, opposing traffic, and queuing require different checks. FHWA road-size limits are not turning templates.

p: Truck dimensions and turning paths
h: Site-review checklist
t: Identify the fleet: exact tractor, trailer, straight-truck, or container/chassis configuration, wheelbases, axle positions, body projections, height, and operating loads. Survey the constraints: gate openings, curb returns, driveways, dock angles, court depth, grade changes, fences, bollards, poles, parked vehicles, easements, fire access, snow storage, and overhead obstructions. Test the maneuver: have a qualified civil/transportation engineer perform fleet-specific swept-path analysis for entry, turns, backing, unloading, and exit, including required operational margins and conflicts. Check access and operation: local truck routes, bridge/underpass restrictions, delivery rules, pavement capacity, loading equipment, and municipal approvals. Legal road width or nominal cargo size is not a guaranteed safe clearance. Apply this reference with the building evaluation checklist , building specifications , and industrial due-diligence guide .

h: RECs, HRECs, and CRECs
t: A recognized environmental condition (REC) indicates likely presence or release of hazardous substances or petroleum. A historical recognized environmental condition (HREC) generally indicates a past release addressed to the applicable standard. A controlled recognized environmental condition (CREC) generally means a past release remains subject to controls, restrictions, or obligations. These terms can affect lender review, buyer obligations, and future use.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Phase II sampling and vapor intrusion
t: A Phase II may sample soil, groundwater, soil gas, indoor air, or other media to test specific concerns. It cannot prove that no risk exists anywhere on the property. Review vapor intrusion where volatile chemicals or petroleum releases may migrate into buildings. Qualified environmental professionals should address sampling methods, seasonal conditions, building pressure, and mitigation design.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Asbestos, lead, PCBs, USTs, and other regulated materials
t: Older industrial buildings may need separate surveys for asbestos, lead paint, PCBs in equipment or caulk, underground and aboveground tanks, hydraulic lifts, sumps, and floor drains. These are often outside a basic Phase I unless added. Ask whether targeted surveys are needed before demolition, renovation, financing, or occupancy. Removal and disposal rules affect timing and cost.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Illinois EPA SRP and NFR letters
t: The Illinois EPA Site Remediation Program is a voluntary cleanup program that can lead to a No Further Remediation letter for addressed conditions. An NFR letter is not the same as saying every environmental risk is gone. Review the recorded terms, institutional controls, engineered barriers, exposure routes, and future-use limits. Counsel and the consultant should confirm whether the proposed use remains consistent with the closure.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Landowner liability protections
t: Federal landowner liability protections are concept-based and fact-specific. They may depend on proper AAI, continuing obligations, no affiliation issues, and conduct after acquisition. Do not treat a report alone as a guarantee. Review the facts with environmental counsel before relying on any protection.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental

t: Turn inspection notes into a capital plan with timing, cost ranges, responsibility, and business impact. Separate immediate life-safety work from maintenance and future improvements.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Title, survey, and land
t: Title and survey connect legal rights to physical use. The title commitment lists requirements and exceptions; the ALTA survey shows boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and encroachments. Review access rights, shared drives, cross-parking, utilities, drainage easements, signage, covenants, and reciprocal easements. A truck entrance across another parcel needs documented rights, not just historical use. For rail-served property, confirm agreements, switch rights, track maintenance, active service, clearance, and who controls access. Rail value depends on legal and physical service rights matching the marketing description.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Zoning and permits
t: Confirm zoning district, permitted and special uses, variances, nonconforming rights, outdoor storage, parking, truck routing, screening, signage, and hours. A zoning verification letter can document the municipality's view. Permits and certificates of occupancy document approved work and uses. Check open permits, violations, expired approvals, fire-code issues, unpermitted mezzanines, and tenant improvements needing closeout. For local research starting points, use the nine-county hub and municipal records. For Chicago-specific research, see the Chicago commercial real estate guide .

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Operational and lease diligence for leased industrial
t: Verify rent-roll income, obligations, and operating rights against signed documents. Request every lease, amendment, guaranty, side letter, estoppel, SNDA, and occupancy notice. Estoppels: confirm rent, term, deposits, defaults, options, exclusive rights, and tenant claims. SNDAs: coordinate lender, buyer, and tenant rights after a foreclosure or ownership change. CAM reconciliations: test recoveries, caps, exclusions, reserves, management fees, and year-end balances. Repair obligations: identify who pays for roof, structure, HVAC, pavement, dock equipment, fire protection, and capital replacements. Hazardous materials clauses: compare lease rights to actual operations, permits, storage, and environmental reports. Parking and trailer rights: confirm allocated spaces, yard rights, storage limits, and rules for containers or fleet vehicles. The commercial leasing guide explains why lease labels do not replace a clause-by-clause review.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Utilities and infrastructure
t: Compare electricity, gas, water, sanitary and storm sewer, compressed air, fiber, and telecom with the user's equipment and occupancy schedule before commitment. Electrical capacity may involve ComEd , the serving utility, an electrical engineer, and the equipment vendor. Confirm voltage, phase, amperage, transformer ownership, spare capacity, upgrade lead times, and shutdown requirements. For existing or proposed battery energy storage, collect ownership and service contracts, approved plans, utility permissions, commissioning records, safety documentation and removal obligations. The BESS owner guide explains storage, peak savings, engineered backup, fire and insurance review, and standalone storage land leases. Neither a large service nor nearby transmission guarantees interconnection capacity. For gas, water, and sewer, check meter size, pressure, discharge limits, floor drains, pretreatment, process water, fire flow, and municipal capacity. General serviceability does not confirm fiber or telecom.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Turning findings into price, credits, escrows, or repairs
t: Findings should drive a decision: accept risk, renegotiate price, request a credit or escrow, require repairs, modify representations, obtain insurance, or terminate if the contract allows. Sellers should separate documented defects from buyer preferences and speculative upgrades. Buyers should distinguish routine maintenance from issues affecting value, financing, insurability, or lawful use. Support material findings with report pages, photos, contractor proposals, municipal responses, title exceptions, lease clauses, or consultant memos.

h: Does my 1031 replacement get a full new depreciation basis?
t: Not automatically. Deferred gain generally carries into replacement basis; exchanged basis and excess investment have separate depreciation rules. A new price neither erases deferred gain nor guarantees full-price deductions.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can rental losses offset my pension or IRA withdrawals?
t: Generally not for passive losses without an applicable allowance or exception. Pension/IRA income is not passive activity income. Real estate professional status plus material participation and qualifying rental allowances have separate tests.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can cost segregation wipe out the tax on a Roth conversion?
t: Not automatically. Passive depreciation losses generally cannot offset conversions, which can raise MAGI and reduce rental loss allowances. Basis, at risk and other limits may also block deductions. Model usable losses, not total study deductions.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Are dividends passive income that rental losses can offset?
t: Portfolio dividends and interest generally are not Section 469 passive activity income. Income requiring little work may be “passive” colloquially without qualifying for rental loss offsets.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does retirement make me a real estate professional?
t: No. Annual qualifying services generally must exceed 750 hours and half your personal services; rentals separately require material participation as applicable. Retirement, licensing or LLC ownership is not enough.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can a retiree use the $25,000 rental loss allowance?
t: Possibly, with qualifying active participation, ownership and MAGI. For most taxpayers other than married filing separately, it generally phases out at $100,000 to $150,000 of specially defined MAGI. Retirement alone does not qualify.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can rent from my own business absorb my other passive rental losses?
t: Not necessarily. Self rental rules generally make net rent from a business in which you materially participate nonpassive, but do not automatically make rental losses nonpassive. Review ownership, participation and grouping before using offsets.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: What happens to suspended rental losses when I sell?
t: Fully taxable dispositions of the entire activity interest to unrelated persons generally release passive losses, subject to applicable rules. A 1031 generally is not that disposition; grouping, recognized income and installment timing can change results.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: How many years do I depreciate a commercial building?
t: Generally 39 years, straight line with the mid month convention, for ordinary nonresidential real property under GDS. Land is excluded; ADS, eligible components, qualified improvements and special property can differ.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can I avoid later tax by never claiming depreciation?
t: Generally no. Allowed or allowable depreciation reduces adjusted basis even if unclaimed. Have a CPA review records and correction procedures rather than deliberately skipping deductions.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Is cost segregation worthwhile near retirement?
t: Compare usable deductions, study cost, carryforwards, hold period, state differences and later recapture. Passive owners may only create suspended losses; near term sales can shorten timing benefits. It is not universally beneficial.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can I write off my whole warehouse with 100% bonus depreciation?
t: No, not an ordinary warehouse purchase under Section 168(k). Eligible shorter life components and improvements may qualify under current rules; land and ordinary 39 year buildings generally do not. Review specialized production property rules separately.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does a new cost segregation study make an old building eligible for new bonus rules?
t: No. Study dates do not reset acquisition or placed in service dates. Review eligible classifications, historical law and any accounting method change for the original assets.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Is all depreciation recapture taxed at 25%?
t: No. Section 1245 ordinary recapture, Section 1250 ordinary recapture and unrecaptured Section 1250 gain differ. The latter's maximum individual rate is 25%, not a mandatory flat rate. Classification, gain, netting and owner type matter.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does paying off my mortgage reduce taxable sale gain?
t: Ordinary loan payoff reduces cash, not generally property gain. Gain depends on amount realized, applicable sale costs and adjusted basis. Loan principal is not tax basis.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can seller financing defer depreciation recapture?
t: Recapture generally is recognized in the sale year even with installment treatment of other eligible gain. Seller financing adds buyer credit, interest and liquidity issues. Review the full transaction before claiming deferral.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does Illinois allow the same immediate federal bonus deduction?
t: Not automatically. Illinois uses IL-4562 addition/subtraction modifications and related returns. Keep separate state/federal depreciation schedules; review current asset, year and disposition rules.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does being retired exempt my Illinois rent or property sale gain?
t: No. Eligible retirement account distributions can qualify for an Illinois subtraction. Retirement does not turn ordinary rent or directly realized property gain into retirement plan income.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: If I move away, do Illinois taxes on my building disappear?
t: No. Illinois source rent, gains and Illinois situs estate property can remain relevant for nonresidents. Have affected-state advisers review sourcing, residency, credits, entity treatment and estate apportionment.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can a building sale raise my Medicare premiums?
t: Yes. Taxable income can affect IRMAA, generally based on a return two years earlier, separately from sale income tax. Qualifying life changing events may support reconsideration; sales alone do not automatically qualify.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Can IRA withdrawals raise net investment income tax on rent?
t: Yes. Retirement distributions generally are not net investment income but can raise MAGI, increasing rental/investment income subject to 3.8% NIIT under applicable activity and threshold rules.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does Illinois have an inheritance tax on my children's building?
t: Illinois currently has estate tax, not separate inheritance tax. Estates may owe tax before distributions; heirs can owe income tax on later rent, sales or taxable inherited account withdrawals. Other states may differ.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: What are the federal and Illinois estate exclusions in 2026?
t: Federal: $15 million per individual for 2026 under current law, affected by prior taxable gifts and other rules. Illinois: separate $4 million exclusion, no state portability. Building equity alone does not determine estate tax.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does a married couple automatically get twice the Illinois estate exclusion?
t: No. Illinois has no portability of unused spousal exclusion. Federal portability requires a separate election, generally on Form 706. Estate planning, marital deductions and trust elections need individual legal review.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Will my children get a new tax basis for inherited property?
t: Qualifying inherited property generally gets fair market value basis at death or applicable alternate value, stepping up or down. Direct property, entity interests, trusts and retirement accounts differ; not every underlying asset gets new basis.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Should I gift my building now to avoid inheritance taxes?
t: There is no universal answer. Lifetime gifts generally carry donor basis for gain and can use gift exclusion or require returns; debt and control changes add issues. Compare estate exposure, income tax basis, family goals and liquidity with counsel before transferring.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does an inherited IRA building get the same step up as personally held property?
t: No ordinary inherited property basis adjustment applies to taxable traditional IRA distributions, which are income in respect of a decedent. Analyze account holdings, basis and beneficiary distribution rules separately.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Do unused passive rental losses pass to my heirs?
t: Not automatically. At death, suspended passive losses generally are deductible only above the relevant inherited basis increase, not passed on as heir carryforwards. Review the final return and other loss limits.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Does putting the building into a living trust remove estate tax?
t: Revocable living trusts generally neither remove property from the owner's taxable estate nor reset lifetime basis. They can help administration and succession. Tax results depend on trust, ownership, powers and estate rules.

p: Commercial real estate taxes for retiring owners
h: Is exchange and hold until death always the best retirement strategy?
t: No. Basis treatment at death is one factor. Liquidity, tenant/sponsor risk, management, fees, estate tax, family preferences and future law can outweigh deferral. Compare taxable sales and other choices; inheritance does not guarantee tax elimination.

p: How is net operating income calculated for commercial property?
h: What is NOI, and what is included?
t: Net operating income = effective gross income (EGI) minus operating expenses. Start with scheduled rent at full occupancy on the chosen lease or market-rent basis. Subtract vacancy, free rent and collection losses; add other property income and tenant recoveries. Reconcile to the rent roll, signed amendments, receivables and general ledger. Typical expenses are real estate taxes, building insurance, owner-paid utilities, repairs, maintenance, contracted services and management. When comparing professionally managed investments, include a supported management allowance even if the owner self-manages. Owner business revenue, tenant sales, refundable deposits and loan proceeds are not property rental income. NOI usually excludes mortgage principal and interest, depreciation, owner income taxes, acquisition costs, tenant improvements, leasing commissions and major capital replacements. Replacement reserves may sit below NOI or enter a lender-adjusted measure. State and reconcile the convention; do not compare incompatible figures.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: How do you build a property cash-flow projection?
t: Set a valuation date and hold period. Project each tenant’s contractual rent, options and expirations; show recoveries, taxes, insurance, repairs and management separately. At rollover, model retention or vacancy, downtime, free rent, supported new rent, tenant improvements (TI) and leasing commissions (LC). Do not deduct vacancy twice by reducing rent and adding the same loss again. Property cash flow is more than NOI : subtract capital replacements and leasing costs when incurred, and state reserve treatment. In a 10,000-100,000-SF building, one tenant departure or roof project can dominate a year. Use condition reports and lease abstracts, not a universal rent-growth rate. Model unlevered cash flow before financing. For equity, add loan proceeds to acquisition funding, subtract hold-period debt service, and deduct payoff and finance charges at sale. Match the discount rate and return label to the cash flows. Pre-tax and after-tax are separate models.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: Discount rate versus cap rate: what is the difference?
t: The discount rate translates future cash into today’s dollars at an assumed required return. A cap rate divides one year’s income by value. An exit cap is a future resale assumption, commonly applied to the next year’s stabilized NOI at the hold’s end. These rates are not interchangeable or necessarily equal. For end-of-year cash flow, present value = cash flow / (1 + discount rate) year . Net present value (NPV) subtracts the initial investment from discounted receipts. Positive NPV means the modeled investment exceeds the chosen return requirement on these assumptions, not that the outcome is certain. IRR is the rate that makes NPV zero. Later negative outlays can produce multiple or unhelpful IRRs; dated cash flows also differ from simple annual periods. Keep NPV, required capital and downside exposure visible even when IRR looks attractive.

h: DCF worked example: operating cash, reversion and present value
t: Illustration only, not market data, an appraisal or an investment recommendation. Assumptions: three-year unlevered hold, end-of-year receipts, no income taxes and an 8% discount rate. Assumed annual dollars; capital and leasing cash outlays below NOI Year NOI Capital / TI / LC Operating cash 1 $200,000 $50,000 $150,000 2 $210,000 $30,000 $180,000 3 $220,000 $30,000 $190,000 Assume year-4 NOI of $230,000 and a 7% exit cap. Gross year-3 reversion = $230,000 / 0.07 = $3,285,714.29; after assumed 2% sale costs, net reversion is $3,220,000. Year-3 total cash is $3,410,000, including $190,000 operating cash. Year-4 NOI prices the sale but is not received again during the hold. Present value = $150,000 / 1.08 + $180,000 / 1.08 2 + $3,410,000 / 1.08 3 = $3,000,177.82 . With $3,000,000 all-in initial investment, NPV is $177.82; at $3,100,000, NPV is negative $99,822.18. Results depend entirely on assumptions and cash timing.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: How do exit cap, rent and downtime change the result?
t: At $230,000 year-4 NOI, illustrative gross resale is $3,833,333 at a 6% exit cap, $3,285,714 at 7% and $2,875,000 at 8%, rounded to dollars before sale costs. A higher exit cap lowers resale at the same income. None is a Chicago market claim. Model discount/exit-rate combinations and a separate operating downside: lower collected rent, higher tax and insurance, longer downtime, larger TI/LC, capital overruns and delayed sale. Rent growth and a lower exit cap are not guaranteed benefits. In a levered case, include refinancing maturity and required additional equity, not just revised return. Direct capitalization is a useful NOI/cap-rate snapshot for stabilized income. DCF exposes changes and execution costs, but detail cannot make speculative assumptions reliable. Have an appraiser and financial/tax advisers review property-specific inputs and conventions.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: Owner questions and answers
t: Is the discount rate the same as the cap rate? No. A discount rate values a series of future cash flows; a cap rate relates one year of NOI to value. An exit cap rate is a future resale assumption. Does a high IRR prove a good real estate investment? No. IRR depends on cash timing and assumptions, can be misleading for nonconventional cash flows, and does not measure absolute capital at risk. Review NPV, required equity and downside cases. Should DCF include mortgage payments? Include debt service and loan payoff in a levered equity model, not in an unlevered property model. Match the discount rate to the cash-flow basis.

Check utility-program eligibility before ordering work. Savings and tenant recoveries affect owner NOI differently. Photovoltaic panels on the Rose Calendars factory roof. Evaluate energy projects against actual bills, equipment condition and lease responsibilities. p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: Which operating costs should an owner review first?
t: Collect at least a year of bills and contracts. Separate recurring expenses, one-time repairs, capital replacements and tenant-paid amounts. Compare cost per relevant square foot, consumption, operating hours and occupancy; a heated manufacturing building is not comparable to an unheated storage shed. See budgeting and normalized expense comparisons . Track each action, responsible party, implementation cost, evidence-based benefit, lease recovery, approval and follow-up measure. Check for duplicate invoices, incorrect meters, services billed to vacant areas, expired promotional pricing and auto-renewals. A charge is not automatically recoverable from tenants.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: How can industrial owners reduce energy and utility waste?
t: Review interval electricity, demand charges, seasonal gas use, and supply and delivery charges. Confirm the tariff with the utility: cheaper commodity quotes may have fees or unfavorable renewal terms. Demand reduction depends on when peaks occur, not just annual kilowatt-hours. Ask qualified contractors about LEDs and controls, occupancy scheduling, office HVAC setpoints, dock seals and weather-stripping. Match controls to tasks, hours and equipment. Preserve required emergency lighting, ventilation, fire and freeze protection. Check water/sewer bills for leaks, irrigation timing, meter errors and locally permitted adjustments; sewer charges do not simply disappear. Check the official ComEd business savings portal and Nicor Gas business efficiency resources . Offers depend on account, territory, measure and current rules. Before purchase, confirm eligibility, approved equipment, preapproval, deadlines and whether landlord or tenant applies. No rebate, approval or savings percentage is promised. Simple payback = net project cost / supported annual savings. Include installation, commissioning, disruption and maintenance; count rebates only if eligible and approved. A project may lower tenant costs or improve resilience without immediately increasing owner NOI.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: Preventive maintenance versus deferred repairs
t: Track roof sections, HVAC, docks, pavement, drains and life-safety systems by condition, warranty, maintenance responsibility and next inspection. Qualified inspections can distinguish repair from replacement and schedule work around tenants. Deferring leaks or clogged drains can increase damage, not save money. Use a multi-year roof, HVAC and paving plan; compare scopes, restoration, permit responsibilities and warranties. Do not cut required fire-system testing, access, structural repairs or worker safety. Engineering and municipal requirements govern the work.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: How do service rebids and management fees reduce waste?
t: Rebid waste, landscaping, snow, janitorial, security and maintenance at identical service levels. Specify frequency, disposal fees, after-hours response, snow triggers, de-icing, insurance, reporting and escalation. A low bid may cost more if it excludes emergencies or transfers uninsured risk. Compare management fees with scope: collections, reporting, lease administration, capital supervision and extra charges. Check invoice approval and related-party vendors. Compare the fee base and services, not just the percentage. Calendar renewals before cancellation windows close.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: How can an owner reduce CAM disputes and improve recoveries?
t: For each lease, record pro rata share and area basis, included costs, exclusions, caps, management fees, capital-amortization permissions, gross-ups, expense stops, reconciliation deadline and audit rights. Allocate once, keep invoices, reconcile estimates to permitted actual costs, return credits and explain increases. Reduce CAM by removing waste and billing accurately, not shifting excluded costs. Caps or vacant shares may leave savings with either party. Show expense reductions and lower recoveries in the NOI bridge before claiming a benefit. Have counsel review disputed clauses and changes. For major cost categories, see the Illinois property-tax appeal and budgeting guide and insurance renewal/risk checklist ; their deadlines, evidence and trade-offs differ from vendor bids.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: A repeatable cost-control cycle
t: Record the baseline bill, service scope and owner/tenant allocation. Get comparable proposals and approvals before changing service. Track implementation cost separately from approved incentives. Compare later consumption and invoices, adjusting for weather or occupancy where relevant. Reconcile recoveries and update the next budget. Illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast: a $6,000 annual invoice reduction less $2,000 unreimbursed implementation cost yields $4,000 first-year net cash before other effects. If tenants reimburse the full recurring expense, owner NOI may not rise by $6,000.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: Owner questions and answers
t: How do I reduce CAM charges without cutting essential service? Audit scope, invoices and lease allocations; rebid comparable services and remove duplicate or ineligible charges. Do not cut required safety work or bill tenants for excluded costs. Do LED upgrades automatically qualify for ComEd incentives? No. Confirm the account, measure, equipment and current program requirements, including any preapproval, before purchase or installation. Does every expense reduction increase property value? No. Tenant reimbursements can fall along with expenses, and service cuts can harm risk or occupancy. Calculate the net owner income effect and capital cost first.

p: Commercial property insurance: an owner renewal checklist
h: Replacement cost, ACV and coinsurance: why do they matter?
t: The Illinois Department of Insurance defines actual cash value (ACV) as replacement cost less depreciation for age and condition. Replacement cost covers like-kind/quality replacement without that deduction, subject to policy terms. Land, investment value and purchase price do not set the building’s reconstruction limit. Review values with a qualified reconstruction estimate and licensed adviser. Building area, construction, systems, location, debris removal and code upgrades matter. Confirm repair/replacement requirements, deadlines and any limits or sublimits on recovery. Coinsurance requires insurance at a specified amount relative to the policy’s valuation basis; underinsurance can reduce even a partial-loss payment. Read the contract for the percentage and ACV/replacement-cost basis. Do not assume a universal percentage or calculate a penalty from purchase price. Review agreed-value provisions and conditions; they are not automatic protection.

p: Commercial property insurance: an owner renewal checklist
h: How should owners compare deductibles and exclusions?
t: Check whether deductibles are flat or percentage-based and what value the percentage uses. Wind/hail, flood, earthquake and water may have separate terms. Model cash exposure for multiple events, not just annual premium; lease reimbursements and lender rules may limit choices. Review vacancy/unoccupancy conditions, sprinkler/alarm safeguards, roof limits, and contamination or wear exclusions. Tell the adviser about occupancy, stored commodities and operational changes. An older roof or changed tenant use warrants review, not a promised premium change.

p: Commercial property insurance: an owner renewal checklist
h: What should leases and tenant COIs require?
t: Have counsel and the licensed adviser coordinate limits, additional-insured status, waivers of subrogation, primary/noncontributory wording where appropriate, evidence deadlines and deductible responsibility. The lease and endorsed policy control; a certificate of insurance (COI) does not amend coverage. Track renewal/cancellation information as required by each policy, confirm named entities and premises, and check contractor coverage before work. A tenant COI does not insure the owner’s building or replace owner liability protection. See lease allocation review when responsibilities are unclear.

p: Commercial property insurance: an owner renewal checklist

Ask qualified advisers about roof, drainage, fire protection, security and maintenance; get carrier feedback before spending for a hoped-for discount. Compare quotes at identical values, limits, deductibles, perils, income periods and exclusions; record differences. Check retained risk and lender/lease constraints before raising deductibles or removing coverage. Record the policy, endorsements, claims contacts and renewal date in the operating budget and reserve plan . No premium benchmark or savings is promised. Rates and coverage depend on the building, use, history and insurer. A licensed professional should recommend coverage; this is education, not insurance or legal advice.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: What belongs in a commercial operating budget?
t: Use actual invoices, signed leases and a monthly trailing statement. Budget base rent, recoveries, collection loss and ancillary income by tenant. Track taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs, snow, waste, grounds, management and other recurring services; schedule renewals and seasonal bills when cash is due, with an annual comparison. For Chicagoland industrial assets, review winter service and heat, roof/drains, loading equipment and paving alongside tenancy. Separate tenant-paid utilities from landlord service. Include tax notices, appeal status and insurance-renewal assumptions instead of extrapolating a quiet year. Monthly, compare budget with actual, explain price, usage and timing variances, update collections and forecast the year. Tax refunds and insurance recoveries are not recurring income. The NOI reconciliation preserves the operating basis; a cash forecast shows liquidity timing.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: How do I benchmark operating expenses without misleading comparisons?
t: Define whether cost per square foot uses rentable, occupied or gross area. Compare property type, heated area, tenant use, service level, period and gross/net lease basis. Separate capital and one-time costs. Utility use per operating hour or occupied area may reveal more than dollars alone. Use normalized history, comparable vendor scopes and verified peer data. This guide provides no Chicago expense ratios or market rates. A low ratio may reflect deferred maintenance, tenant-paid costs or missing management fees, not efficiency. Label sources and adjustments.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: Capex versus opex: where do roof and HVAC costs go?
t: Separate owner reporting questions from tax classification Item Owner cash / underwriting view Review needed Routine servicing Typically recurring operating expense Lease responsibility and accounting policy Major roof/system replacement Separate capital plan and cash outlay Condition, scope, permits and CPA classification TI and leasing commission Leasing cash needs below ordinary NOI Lease timing, amortization and tax treatment Reserve deposit Cash earmarked for future needs, not the repair itself Lender convention, funding and access restrictions Federal IRS tangible-property rules distinguish ordinary expenses from capitalized amounts, including betterments, restorations and adaptations. Dollar size alone does not decide classification. Safe harbors and elections have conditions; do not relabel improvements as repairs to reduce NOI or taxable income.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: How much reserve cash does a commercial owner need?
t: No universal percentage ensures an adequate reserve. Schedule asset condition, timing, estimated installed replacement cost, lease responsibility and contingency. Add vacancy carrying costs, TI/LC, deductibles, tax timing and loan maturity. Separate lender-restricted reserves from cash available promptly. Illustrative arithmetic, not a reserve recommendation: a supported $120,000 project estimate, $20,000 already dedicated and five years to completion imply $20,000 annual straight-line funding before inflation, interest or contingencies. An earlier failure requires cash sooner. Do not count both annual contributions and the eventual project as expenses in the same cash-flow model.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: Depreciation, cost segregation and 1031: what should I ask my CPA?
t: Depreciation allocates eligible capital basis over its recovery period; it is not current-year cash spending and is excluded from ordinary property NOI. Land is not depreciable. Basis allocation, placed-in-service dates, classification, elections and current law matter. See IRS Publication 946 , not a promised deduction. A cost-segregation study identifies supported components and tax classifications/recovery periods; it is neither an automatic percentage write-off nor an operating expense. Ask about study quality, basis reconciliation, timing, costs and recapture on sale. The IRS audit-guide directory links the Cost Segregation guide and warns that law may change after publication. Section 1031 may defer, not erase, qualifying gain on business/investment real-property exchanges. Property held primarily for sale does not qualify; cash or other non-like-kind property may create taxable gain. Before closing, discuss ownership, qualified-intermediary arrangements, identification and completion deadlines, debt and state taxes. See sale/1031 preparation and the IRS real-estate exchange overview . Consult a CPA and attorney; no tax result is promised.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: Refinancing and debt costs belong in the liquidity plan
t: Track interest, amortization, fees, escrows, covenants, maturity, recourse and prepayment. DSCR compares a lender-defined income measure with debt service; LTV compares debt with its value basis; debt yield compares defined NOI with loan balance. No universal qualifying threshold applies. Planned refinancing does not erase a balloon balance. Test lower proceeds, higher borrowing costs and delayed closing; calculate the post-payoff, post-fee cash gap. Use the existing debt-service calculator and financing guide and levered versus unlevered projections , not a duplicate calculator.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: Owner questions and answers
t: What is included in commercial operating expenses? Typically taxes, property insurance, owner-paid utilities, recurring repairs/services and management. Debt service, depreciation and major capital outlays are separate from ordinary NOI. State reserve and lease-recovery conventions. Are reserves the same as capital spending? No. A reserve earmarks cash; capital spending pays for work. A lender can treat reserves differently in underwriting, so reconcile the convention and avoid double-counting. Does cost segregation increase NOI? No. It concerns tax depreciation timing and classification, not rental operating income. Review eligibility, study quality, current law and later recapture with a CPA.

p: Comparing commercial leases in Chicago
h: Gross and net are labels, not complete budgets
t: Gross lease Usually bundles some building expenses into rent; utilities, increases, exclusions and other charges may remain separate. Modified gross lease Allocates expenses by agreement. Confirm what is included and what can change. Net or triple-net (NNN) lease Commonly adds taxes, insurance and maintenance to base rent. The label does not decide responsibility for the roof, structure, capital repairs or every operating cost. Common area maintenance (CAM) Shared property costs; review the lease’s definition, allocation, exclusions, reconciliation and review rights. Confirm whether the quoted rate is annual or monthly, its area basis and currency. Request the expense estimate and supporting history; actual pass-throughs may differ at reconciliation.

p: Comparing commercial leases in Chicago
h: Build a total occupancy-cost comparison
t: Separate recurring, upfront, refundable-security and later capital costs. Compare options over the same lease term and area basis, including scheduled increases. Recurring: base rent, tax and insurance pass-throughs, CAM, utilities, maintenance contracts, parking and other required charges. Upfront: professional review, permits, buildout, equipment installation, relocation and costs not reimbursed by a tenant-improvement allowance. Cash tied up: security deposits, prepaid rent and letters of credit. Refundable security ties up liquidity but is not automatically an operating expense. Contingent: expense increases, tenant-assigned major repairs, delayed delivery, exit restoration and costs of changing operations. Illustrative arithmetic only, not Chicago market data. If 10,000 rentable square feet were quoted at $12 per square foot per year in base rent and $4 in estimated annual pass-throughs, those two components would total $160,000 per year, or about $13,333 per month. Utilities, improvements, other charges, and future changes would still need to be added. This example is not an available property or a rent estimate. Ask for each figure’s basis. Label unknowns as estimates and test a higher-cost case rather than treating them as zero.

p: Comparing commercial leases in Chicago
h: A lease-review checklist
t: Premises and use: verify the space, shared areas, permitted use, parking, loading, yard rights and operating restrictions. Term and delivery: distinguish possession, rent commencement, substantial completion and conditions to operate. Improvements: document scope, approvals, allowance, reimbursement conditions, overruns, ownership and removal obligations. Repairs: allocate ordinary maintenance and major HVAC, roof, structural, pavement and fire-protection work. Expenses: review allocation percentages, exclusions, negotiated caps, reconciliation and document-review rights. Risk: have counsel review insurance, indemnity, casualty, condemnation, default remedies and any personal guaranty. Flexibility: check renewal options and notice deadlines, assignment, subleasing, expansion, termination and restoration. A letter of intent can organize negotiations, but its binding effect depends on wording and circumstances. Have counsel review it before signing; do not assume every term is nonbinding.

p: Comparing commercial leases in Chicago
h: Make the occupancy schedule credible
t: Check zoning and building requirements before setting a move-in date; allow for design, permits, utilities, construction, inspections and equipment commissioning. For industrial space, review loading, power, storage and fire-protection suitability early because each affects cost and timing. Write down who delivers each item, proof of completion and the consequence of delay. Confirm the schedule with authorities and contractors; “available now” does not mean ready for your business.
