p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
t: Research guide Researching Chicago commercial real estate A commercial property search becomes more useful when it starts with a proposed use and a verification plan. An address, an asking price, and a listing description are not enough to establish whether a building can support your business or investment. Educational guide, not a market report. Talk about your building Questions about selling an industrial building? Contact Pavlo Rospopa at Marcus & Millichap. Call (630) 570‑2184 Email pavlo.rospopa@marcusmillichap.com In brief Start from the proposed use and a verification plan, not from an address or asking price. Identify the municipality, county, and every PIN; the zoning authority follows the parcel, not the mailing address. Zoning maps, building records, and tax bills are starting points that need confirmation with the responsible authority and qualified advisers. Compare options on the same basis: area definition, total cost, timing, and verified evidence. Owner lens: Before spending on a conversion, verify the approval path, who pays for utility or off-site work, and what happens to the budget if approvals or occupancy are delayed. Chicago’s Loop from the lakefront. City records cover the city; suburban and unincorporated parcels have their own authorities. Photo: Ryan , CC BY 2.0 ; cropped and converted to monochrome.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 1. Define what the property must do
t: Record the proposed activity, occupancy date, usable area, budget and non-negotiable physical requirements. Separate must-haves from preferences. For a property for sale, identify owner occupancy, rental income or redevelopment; each requires different underwriting. Office Consider layout, accessibility, telecommunications, commuting and adaptation costs. Retail and service space Check customer access, visibility, deliveries, permitted activity, licensing and buildout needs. Industrial and warehouse property Evaluate loading, clear height, power, circulation and operations before comparing area. See the industrial evaluation guide . Flex and mixed-use property Identify each actual use and its share. “Flex” does not establish permission for manufacturing, retail, laboratory or assembly.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 2. Confirm the jurisdiction and parcel
t: “Chicago area” may mean the city or a much larger region. Identify municipality, county, address and every property index number (PIN). A marketing address may cover multiple parcels; a mailing address does not establish the zoning authority. For city property, start with Chicago zoning and building resources. For suburban property, check municipal planning and building departments; for unincorporated parcels, confirm the county authority. Use the parcel’s county assessor and treasurer. Cook County records do not cover DuPage, Lake, Will, Kane or other counties. Log the source, retrieval date, parcel or address, result and open questions. Keep source documents, not just screenshots or search snippets. For industrial property beyond the city, the nine-county Chicagoland industrial hub links county-specific planning, zoning and parcel sources for Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry and Will counties, while distinguishing municipal authority.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 3. Verify use, condition, and obligations
t: Zoning is a starting point Find the zoning designation and describe the proposed operation to the authority. Confirm additional approvals, special uses, parking or loading rules and restrictions. Existing occupancy or a prior tenant’s business does not automatically permit a new operation. Building records need interpretation Review available permits and violations; have qualified advisers investigate open issues. Public records may be incomplete and do not establish roof, structural, electrical, fire-protection or other conditions. Arrange inspections suited to the property and intended use. Taxes are not a fixed listing number Match bills and assessments to the PINs and tax year. Assessed value, tax bill and market value are different. Ask a qualified tax adviser how reassessment, appeals, incentives or a use/ownership change may affect the budget; last year’s bill is not a forecast. Access and environmental questions can change the decision Check access rights, easements, drainage and flood information. Past industrial activity may warrant environmental diligence even when current use appears ordinary. The purchase-diligence guide places these checks in acquisition review.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 4. Put each option on the same basis
t: Area: record the source and whether it is rentable, usable, building or land area. Cost: separate price or base rent from taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, improvements and transaction costs. Timing: include possession, approvals, construction and equipment installation, not just closing or lease dates. Evidence: distinguish verified facts from representations and estimates. Asking terms do not prove a completed transaction or market value. For rental decisions, continue to comparing commercial leases . For an acquisition, continue to investment and purchase diligence .

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: Official research sources
t: City of Chicago zoning map : initial zoning location research; confirm interpretations with the responsible authority. Chicago Department of Buildings : building permits, inspections, and code-enforcement resources. Cook County Assessor : parcel and assessment research. Cook County Treasurer : tax bills and payment information. FEMA Flood Map Service Center : official flood-hazard maps, which do not show every water or drainage problem.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Clear height
t: Usable vertical height from the finished floor to the lowest overhead obstruction.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Column spacing
t: The distance between structural columns, important for racking, staging, equipment, and forklift movement.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Dock-high door
t: A loading door designed for trailers backed to a dock.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Drive-in door
t: A grade-level overhead door that lets vehicles enter the building or yard area.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Truck court
t: Paved area outside dock doors where trucks back, turn, and queue. Evaluate usable depth for the actual fleet and maneuver, not a universal turning radius. See the turning circle, swept-path, and offtracking reference .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Trailer parking
t: Outdoor spaces used to store trailers, subject to zoning, surface, screening, and lease limits.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cross-dock
t: A building arranged for freight to move from inbound doors to outbound doors with limited storage time.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Rail-served
t: A property with rail access or a rail spur; service, rights, and track condition still need review.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: ESFR sprinklers
t: Early Suppression Fast Response sprinklers for certain high-piled storage conditions.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Slab load and flatness
t: Slab capacity and surface tolerance, especially for heavy storage or narrow-aisle systems.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: 3-phase power
t: Industrial electrical service; verify voltage, amperage, transformer capacity, and utility supply.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Mezzanine
t: An intermediate platform or floor inside a building, subject to permits, structure, fire, and egress review.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Office finish %
t: The portion of a building improved as office space.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Flex space
t: A suite or building combining office, showroom, light industrial, storage, or service use.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: IOS (industrial outdoor storage)
t: Land for storing vehicles, equipment, materials, containers, or trailers. Permitted use depends on zoning, screening, surface, access, and environmental controls.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Class A/B/C industrial
t: Informal market labels for relative quality, age, features, location, and tenant appeal.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Land-to-building ratio
t: The relationship between site area and building area.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Site coverage
t: The portion of a parcel covered by buildings and sometimes other impervious improvements.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Infill vs. greenfield
t: Infill sites are in developed areas; greenfields are undeveloped or less-developed land.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: NNN / triple net
t: A lease where the tenant commonly pays base rent, taxes, insurance, and operating expenses.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Gross lease
t: A lease where many property expenses are included in rent.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Modified gross
t: A lease between gross and net structures, with expenses allocated by contract.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: CAM
t: Common-area charges for costs such as snow, landscaping, lighting, security, pavement, and management, subject to lease inclusions, exclusions, caps, and allocation. See CAM reconciliation and cost controls .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Base rent
t: Stated rent before pass-through expenses, credits, abatements, or other adjustments.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Escalations
t: Scheduled rent increases or expense adjustments, fixed, percentage-based, index-based, or tied to operating costs.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: TI allowance
t: Money a landlord contributes toward approved tenant improvements.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: LC (leasing commission)
t: Compensation paid for procuring a tenant or lease renewal; model it as a leasing cash need in the hold-period DCF .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Expense stop
t: A threshold where the landlord covers expenses up to a stated amount and the tenant pays certain increases above it.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Estoppel certificate
t: A tenant statement confirming key lease facts, defaults, deposits, options, and claims.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: SNDA
t: Subordination, non-disturbance, and attornment agreement among tenant, landlord, and lender.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Holdover
t: A tenant remaining after lease expiration, usually subject to lease consequences and remedies.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Renewal option
t: Contractual right to extend a lease if notice, timing, and default conditions are met.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: ROFR / ROFO
t: Rights of first refusal or first offer that may affect sale or leasing flexibility.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: WALT
t: Remaining lease duration weighted by rent or area.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Rent roll
t: Summary of tenants, suites, area, rent, deposits, options, and lease dates.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: EGI (effective gross income)
t: Potential rent less vacancy and credit losses, plus collectible recoveries and other property income, stated annually. See the rent-to-NOI bridge .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: DCF (discounted cash flow)
t: Projection discounting future property or equity cash flows to a valuation date. State capital, lease rollover, and sale assumptions. DCF guide .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: NPV (net present value)
t: Discounted future net receipts minus initial investment at a chosen rate; positive modeled NPV is not guaranteed. Worked example .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Discount rate
t: Required return used to convert future cash to present value, matched to levered or unlevered and pre- or after-tax cash flows. Not a cap rate.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Exit cap rate
t: Future resale capitalization assumption, commonly applied to the year after the hold's NOI. A higher rate lowers indicated resale at the same NOI.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Debt yield
t: Defined annual NOI divided by loan balance; definitions and thresholds vary by lender. Financing comparison .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Capex (capital expenditures)
t: Cash for capital improvements or replacements, generally modeled separately from property NOI. Tax capitalization is a separate analysis.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Opex (operating expenses)
t: Recurring property operating costs on the stated accounting basis, such as taxes, insurance, maintenance and management. Debt service is separate.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Replacement reserve
t: Cash earmarked for future capital needs; funding is not payment for work. State lender and model conventions to avoid double-counting.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Coinsurance
t: A policy provision tying required insurance amounts to a specified value basis and percentage; underinsurance can reduce payment. Actual wording controls. Insurance valuation .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: BI (business income) / loss of rents
t: Insurance for qualifying income losses after a covered event, subject to triggers, time limits, and exclusions; not ordinary vacancy or tenant-default protection.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cook County Class 6b
t: An incentive assessment classification for qualifying industrial development, rehabilitation or reutilization, subject to application, local support and compliance. Compare incentive classes .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: NOI
t: Effective gross property income minus operating expenses, before debt service, depreciation, and major capital needs. State the reserve convention. See NOI calculation and recoveries .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cap rate
t: NOI divided by price or value; a shorthand income and risk measure, not a complete valuation.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Going-in vs. exit cap
t: Going-in cap rate uses current or first-year income; exit cap rate is a resale assumption.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: DSCR
t: Debt service coverage ratio compares income available for debt payments to required debt service.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: LTV
t: Loan-to-value compares loan amount to property value, purchase price, or another lender-defined base.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: IRR
t: Internal rate of return is the discount rate that makes modeled net present value zero. Nonconventional cash flows may have multiple or no useful IRRs. See DCF return measures .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Equity multiple
t: Total cash returned divided by total equity invested.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cash-on-cash
t: Annual cash flow compared with cash invested, often after debt service and before taxes.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Basis
t: May mean tax basis, cost basis, or an investor's all-in cost. Confirm which definition applies.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Replacement cost
t: Estimated cost to build a similar asset today.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Sale-leaseback
t: A transaction where an owner sells a property and leases it back.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Owner-user vs. investor
t: An owner-user buys to occupy; an investor buys for income, appreciation, redevelopment, or resale.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Value-add vs. core
t: Core usually describes stabilized assets with lower perceived risk. Value-add usually involves vacancy, rollover, improvements, repositioning, or other execution risk.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: 1031 exchange
t: Qualifying exchange of business or investment real property that can defer gain. Deferred exchanges generally require identification within 45 days and completion by the earlier of 180 days or the relevant tax-return due date, including extensions, subject to detailed rules. See IRS Form 8824 instructions and owner tax planning . Consult a CPA or attorney before closing.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Qualified intermediary
t: A party used to facilitate a 1031 exchange and hold exchange proceeds.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: LOI
t: A letter of intent outlining business terms before a purchase agreement or lease.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: PSA
t: A purchase and sale agreement governing price, deposits, diligence, conditions, default, and closing.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Due diligence period
t: Agreed time for a buyer to inspect records, title, survey, environmental and physical condition, leases, zoning, and financing.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Earnest money
t: A buyer deposit governed by the PSA and escrow instructions.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: PIN (property index number)
t: A parcel identifier used in county tax and assessment records.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Assessed value & equalization factor
t: Assessed value is a county's property-tax figure, derived from but distinct from market value and the tax bill. The county or Illinois Department of Revenue applies an equalization factor to make assessment levels uniform across jurisdictions. Verify current figures with the assessor and treasurer.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Triennial reassessment
t: Cook County reassesses property on a three-year cycle; verify timing and notices with the county assessor.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Township assessor
t: In most Illinois counties outside Cook, elected official who sets initial property values; the county supervisor of assessments reviews and equalizes them. Contact the county office to find the right township assessor.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Transfer tax
t: A tax that may apply at state, county, or municipal levels when real estate changes ownership.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Zoning map amendment
t: A legislative change to a parcel's zoning classification.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Special use
t: A use allowed only after specific local approval, often with conditions.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Variance
t: Relief from a zoning standard, such as a setback or parking requirement.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Unincorporated vs. incorporated
t: Whether property is outside or inside municipal boundaries, affecting zoning, permits, services, and records.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Enterprise zone
t: A designated area that may offer incentives if a project qualifies; eligibility must be verified.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: TIF district
t: A tax increment financing district that captures certain future tax growth for eligible public purposes.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Phase I ESA / AAI
t: An environmental diligence report; EPA All Appropriate Inquiries guidance explains federal standards.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: ALTA survey
t: A detailed survey used to review boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and title-related survey matters.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Title commitment
t: A title insurer's commitment to issue a policy subject to requirements and exceptions.
